This basal oxygen consumption, typical for a member of the Vespertilionidae of its size, underscores the moderate energetic demands of a foliage-roosting bat that employs daily torpor during cooler periods. At a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], gestation in this species spans approximately 85 days [tg = approximately 85 days], a duration that aligns with the 80 to 90 day range described for many temperate vespertilionids. Females typically enter pregnancy following spring ovulations, and the developing embryo undergoes organogenesis throughout the late spring months. The reliance on a warm thermal regime during gestation is critical, as the foetal growth phase depends on sustained maternal warmth to maintain the temperature necessary for normal embryogenesis. Under these same thermal conditions, litter sizes range from one to four pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = one to four pups per reproductive event], with a single litter produced annually [F_R_i = single litter produced annually], occurring once per year. This reproductive strategy, in which each female produces only one litter per year, means that the annual offspring output is low, but each pup is born at a relatively advanced stage of development.

Neonates at the moment of live birth have a wet mass averaging approximately 1.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.5 grams], a value consistent with the altricial condition common among bats. This modest birth weight reflects the constraints of flight in the gravid female, as the total mass of the litter represents a substantial fraction of her own body mass. Pups are born fully furred but with eyes closed, and they cling tightly to the mother's fur during the first days post-parturition. The suckling juvenile remains dependent on maternal milk for nourishment during the pre-weaning phase, a period of rapid mass gain. The time since birth at weaning, when pups achieve nutritional independence from the mother, is 38 days [tx = 38 days], observed under the same thermal conditions of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] that prevail during the active season. Weaning marks the cessation of consistent milk ingestion and the transition to a diet of aerial insects captured on the wing. After weaning, the juvenile enters a sub-adult phase during which it must refine its foraging skills and accumulate sufficient body reserves to survive its first winter. By mid-to-late summer, the weaned juveniles are fully volant and capable of capturing prey independently, a crucial milestone before the onset of autumn migration or hibernation.

Females of Lasiurus borealis attain an ultimate body mass of approximately 13 grams [Wwi = approximately 13 grams] at sexual maturity, though adult body mass in the field ranges from 7 to 13 grams depending on season, reproductive condition, and prey availability. This mass range is typical for a small foliage-roosting insectivore and places the species among the smaller members of the genus Lasiurus. The attainment of reproductive maturity just over one year after birth ensures that mating occurs before the individual's second winter, allowing it to contribute to the next generation. Young-of-the-year males also undergo testicular descent and spermatogenesis by their first autumn, though they may not sire offspring until the following spring due to the timing of female receptivity. The species thus exhibits a typical temperate-zone life history wherein first-year individuals invest primarily in somatic growth before allocating resources to reproduction.

This translates to roughly 14.5 years, placing Lasiurus borealis in the moderate longevity bracket for a bat of its small size. Among insectivorous bats, lifespans of several years are common, and this species likely benefits from roosting in dense foliar cover, which reduces predation pressure compared to cave-roosting species. The oldest documented individuals in the wild are typically those that have avoided predation and disease during hibernation or winter torpor. During the cold months, individuals seek refuge in leaf litter or tree cavities and enter prolonged bouts of torpor, substantially reducing metabolic demands and presumably contributing to the species' survival over multiple winters. The reproductive output over a lifetime, given the single annual litter and typical survival rates, is modest, and population growth is sensitive to adult female mortality. Understanding the interplay between adult longevity, reproductive rate, and juvenile survival is central to modelling the population dynamics of this migratory species.
